issues.legal_issue: A retrial on an appeal against acquittal cannot be ordered merely to give the prosecution a second opportunity to present evidence it could have presented at trial.
material_facts: The prosecution relied substantially on a disputed letter to support the charge.
The complainant did not call a handwriting expert, although the prosecution had the opportunity to do so and was not denied an opportunity to present evidence.
The trial court found the charge unproved and acquitted the accused.
On appeal, the High Court ordered a retrial so the complainant could call a handwriting expert.
issues.conclusion: The retrial order was erroneous and was set aside; the acquittal stood.
issues.legal_principle: An accused should not ordinarily be tried again for the same offence, except in very exceptional circumstances. An appellate court may reverse an acquittal if the trial court’s assessment is wholly unacceptable, but it should not order a retrial simply to let the prosecution supply evidence it could and should have produced at trial when it was given a fair opportunity. No earlier cases or specific provision governing this point were relied on.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and central_evidence_contested and prosecution_omitted_available_evidence and not prosecution_denied_fair_opportunity

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal from a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.central_evidence_contested: The accused disputed evidence on which the prosecution substantially relied.
predicates.prosecution_omitted_available_evidence: The prosecution did not present evidence that it could have presented at trial.
predicates.prosecution_denied_fair_opportunity: The trial court denied the prosecution a fair opportunity to present the omitted evidence.
predicates.retrial_not_ordered_to_fill_prosecution_: A retrial is not ordered merely to allow the prosecution to fill an evidentiary gap it could have filled at the original trial.

issues.definition: When an acquittal is appealed and the prosecution omitted available evidence despite a fair opportunity to present it, a retrial is not ordered merely to fill that evidentiary gap.

issues.legal_issue: An accused person's professional status and relationship with the complainant do not justify applying different criminal-trial standards or ordering a retrial on that basis.
material_facts: The accused was a practising lawyer engaged by the complainant in connection with a property transaction.
The complainant prosecuted the accused for an alleged breach of trust arising from that transaction.
The High Court relied on the lawyer-client relationship in ordering a retrial.
The High Court was hearing a criminal appeal, not a disciplinary proceeding for professional misconduct.
issues.conclusion: The accused’s status as a lawyer and the prior professional relationship supplied no basis for a retrial; the same rules of criminal jurisprudence applied as in other criminal cases.
issues.legal_principle: The ordinary rules of criminal jurisprudence apply equally to accused persons regardless of profession. Professional status gives neither preferential treatment nor an additional disability, and a criminal proceeding is not a disciplinary proceeding merely because the accused is a professional. No earlier cases or specific provision were relied on for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_acquittal and accused_is_professional and complainant_was_professional_client and proceeding_is_not_disciplinary

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal from an acquittal.
predicates.accused_is_professional: The accused has a professional occupation.
predicates.complainant_was_professional_client: The complainant had engaged the accused in a professional capacity in connection with the underlying matter.
predicates.proceeding_is_not_disciplinary: The proceeding determines criminal liability rather than professional discipline.
predicates.ordinary_criminal_standards_apply_withou: The accused’s professional status and relationship with the complainant do not alter the standards applied in the criminal proceeding.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal from an acquittal that is not disciplinary, an accused’s professional status and prior professional relationship with the complainant do not alter the ordinary criminal standards.
